items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “building artificial structures such as sea walls, groynes and rock armour to control natural processes”.
items.answer: Hard engineering
items.markingKey: Hard engineering: building artificial structures such as sea walls, groynes and rock armour to control natural processes. [1]

items.stem: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of hard and soft engineering.
items.answer: Hard: effective, long-lasting protection of high-value land, but expensive, unattractive, disrupt sediment and shift erosion down-drift. Soft: cheaper, natural, create habitats and adapt to change, but need regular maintenance and may lose land.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed comparison [4]

items.stem: Explain how beach nourishment protects a coastline.
items.answer: A wider, higher beach absorbs wave energy before it reaches the cliffs or sea wall; it also supplies sediment to down-drift beaches; but sediment is lost and must be replaced every few years.

items.stem: Table 8.1 shows options for protecting a 2000 m stretch of coast at a town on the Holderness coast. Cost per metre (£) and expected lifespan (years): managed realignment: £500 per m, 100 years; recurved sea wall: £10 800 per m, 50 years; rock armour: £3 900 per m, 30 years; timber groynes: £1 400 per m, 20 years. Property and infrastructure worth about £80 million is at risk. Calculate the annual cost per metre of each option over its lifespan.
items.answer: managed realignment: £5; recurved sea wall: £216; rock armour: £130; timber groynes: £70
items.markingKey: cost ÷ lifespan [2]

items.stem: Table 8.1 shows options for protecting a 2000 m stretch of coast at a village in West Sussex. (b) Calculate the benefit-cost ratio of recurved sea wall for the whole stretch, taking the benefit as the value of property at risk.
items.answer: (a) £1 400 000 (b) Cost £13.8 million; benefit-cost ratio 40 ÷ 13.8 = 2.9

items.stem: “Soft engineering is the most sustainable approach to coastal management.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to environment and sea-level rise.
items.answer: For: It works with natural processes, adapts to sea-level rise, creates habitats and is cheaper in the long term (Medmerry, Sand Engine). Against: Hard engineering is needed to protect high-value assets and dense populations (Malé seawall, Dutch Delta Works); soft schemes need repeated maintenance and may sacrifice land and homes. Conclusion: Soft engineering is more sustainable where land values are low, but a mix of approaches is needed on developed coasts.

items.answer: Not correct. It often moves the problem down-drift and can fail in severe storms.

items.stem: Explain why managed realignment is increasingly used.
items.answer: Rising sea level and the cost of maintaining defences; the salt marsh created absorbs wave energy and provides habitat; cheaper long-term than holding the line (e.g. Medmerry, 2013).

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “managing the whole coastal zone, land and sea, in a coordinated way that involves all stakeholders and considers environmental, economic and social needs”.
items.answer: Integrated coastal zone management (ICZM)
items.markingKey: Integrated coastal zone management (ICZM): managing the whole coastal zone, land and sea, in a coordinated way that involves all stakeholders and considers environmental, economic and social needs. [1]

items.stem: Explain why coastal management should be integrated.
items.answer: Coastal processes link places within a sediment cell, so defences in one place affect others; many stakeholders compete for coastal resources; land and sea issues interact; long-term planning for sea-level rise is needed.

items.stem: Explain why there are conflicts over shoreline management decisions.
items.answer: Residents and businesses want protection; government must balance cost against benefit; conservation groups want natural processes; down-drift communities lose sediment; insurers and farmers have different interests.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that integrated coastal zone management is easier to plan than to achieve? In your answer you may refer to stakeholders and sea-level rise.
items.answer: For: ICZM principles are widely adopted (EU recommendation 2002, SMPs) and give a logical, cell-based, long-term framework. Against: Conflicts between stakeholders, limited funding, compensation problems for people whose homes are not protected, political pressure and different administrative boundaries hinder implementation. Conclusion: The concept is sound, but funding, conflicting interests and political pressure make full integration hard to achieve.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “integrated coastal zone management (ICZM)”?
options: An SMP policy of maintaining the existing position of the shoreline by defences.
A plan for a sediment cell or sub-cell that sets a management policy for each stretch of coast in England and Wales.
An SMP policy of not investing in defences and allowing natural processes to continue.
Managing the whole coastal zone, land and sea, in a coordinated way that involves all stakeholders and considers environmental, economic and social needs.

items.stem: Explain why the Holderness coast is difficult to manage sustainably.
items.answer: Very rapid erosion of soft boulder clay (about 1.8 m a year); defending one place starves down-drift beaches; low-value farmland makes defences hard to justify; gas terminal at Easington and villages need protection.

items.stem: Explain why managed realignment at Medmerry is considered sustainable.
items.answer: It protects about 350 homes and roads more cheaply in the long term than maintaining the shingle bank; it creates intertidal habitat, offsetting coastal squeeze; it works with natural processes.

items.stem: Using one named example of the management of a stretch of coastline, evaluate how sustainable the management has been.

items.stem: “Coastal management can never be fully sustainable.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to managed realignment, stakeholders and sea-level rise.
items.answer: For: Defences shift problems down-drift, need repeated maintenance and cause coastal squeeze; rising sea level will make many defences unaffordable. Conclusion: Full sustainability is difficult, but approaches that work with natural processes and plan for sea-level rise come closest.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that soft engineering is the most sustainable approach to coastal management?
items.answer: For: It works with natural processes, adapts to sea-level rise, creates habitats and is cheaper in the long term (Medmerry, Sand Engine). Against: Hard engineering is needed to protect high-value assets and dense populations (Malé seawall, Dutch Delta Works); soft schemes need repeated maintenance and may sacrifice land and homes. Conclusion: Soft engineering is more sustainable where land values are low, but a mix of approaches is needed on developed coasts.

items.stem: “Coastal management can never be fully sustainable.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to hard engineering, stakeholders and managed realignment.
items.answer: For: Defences shift problems down-drift, need repeated maintenance and cause coastal squeeze; rising sea level will make many defences unaffordable. Against: Managed realignment (Medmerry), mega-nourishment (Sand Engine) and ICZM work with natural processes and adapt to change; mangrove restoration provides protection and livelihoods. Conclusion: Full sustainability is difficult, but approaches that work with natural processes and plan for sea-level rise come closest.
